claude.sample_unit: case-prompt classifications (70 synthetic vignettes x 3 prompting strategies)

links.outcome: Accuracy of NHSN classification across standard, structured, and constrained prompts
links.effect: Overall accuracy rose from 78.6% (standard) to 88.6% (structured) and 95.7% (constrained); Cochran's Q(2)=18.2, P<.001; false-positive rate fell from 33.3% to 7.1%.
links.quote: The constrained (95.7%) and structured (88.6%) prompts showed higher accuracy than the standard (78.6%) prompt (McNemar P = .00049 and P = .0156, respectively).

links.outcome: LLM classification accuracy against gold-standard NHSN definitions, including false positives
links.effect: Overall accuracy 87.6% (184/210) with 25 false positives and 1 false negative; lowest for CDI (81.0%) and CLABSI (80.4%); model overcalled infections.
links.quote: Consistent with prior work, these findings indicate that LLMs tend to overcall HAIs: they are overly sensitive and insufficiently specific.

links.outcome: Incorrect LLM classifications that would require clinician verification
links.effect: 26 misclassified vignettes; errors in exclusion rules, quantitative thresholds, and hierarchical attribution persisted even under constrained prompting (constrained accuracy 95.7%). Authors conclude human oversight is needed.
links.quote: Taken together, these findings suggest that LLMs of this kind require human oversight and are not yet ready for fully autonomous deployment in HAI surveillance.

links.outcome: Suitability of LLM output as stand-alone surveillance classification
links.effect: Model overcalled HAIs with false positives 33.3% under standard prompt and 7.1% constrained; authors state it cannot function as an autonomous HAI surveillance tool, only as decision-support with human final decisions.
links.quote: Currently, GPT-5.1 Thinking cannot function as an autonomous HAI surveillance tool.

unlisted_practices: Using structured or constrained rule-checking prompts to improve adherence of LLMs to formal definitions
